newsitem.title: USA: Local consumers a little more cautious - Phil. Fed.
newsitem.headline: Local consumers a little more cautious - Phil. Fed.

text.p: Consumers in the third U.S. economic district are a little more careful when it comes to spending their dollars than they were a few months ago, an official at the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia said.

"I think people are a little more cautious than they were a few months ago. It's not that they're not spending, (but) they're a little cautious," Ted Crone, vice president and head of the regional economics section of the Philadelphia Fed, told Reuters.

Crone said he expects growth in the third district, which encompasses Delaware, the eastern region of Pennsylvania and the southern portion of New Jersey, to slow in the second quarter from the torrid levels seen in the first three months of the year.
"The first quarter is probably going stand out this year as the best quarter in terms of growth. I think from now on things will slow down a little bit, especially in the housing sector," Crone said.
The Philadelphia Fed economist said housing permits and starts in the region benefited from good weather in the first quarter, but they were expected to slow somewhat in the second one.
"I think now we sort of basically have a little drift downwards in terms of housing permits. But that's from a high level," Crone said.
The Philadelphia Fed vice president also said labor markets in the third region were still tight, but added that the rate of employment growth was seen moderating.
"We had a good pick up in jobs in the first quarter, but our overall year-over-year (job) growth rate doesn't look as strong as the first quarter on an annualized basis," he said.
"I think that at this point our growth rates will moderate a bit," he added.

Crone also said he expects the share of the manufacturing sector in the region's economy to diminish over the next five to 10 years as costs involved in opening new plants in the region have increased over the last several years.
Crone, who conducted an extensive study about manufacturing jobs in the third regional economy, also said increases in productivity have not historically been matched by gains in the number of jobs.
"Our share (of manufacturing) will probably diminish over the ... next five to 10 years," Crone said.

"And over that time, we don't expect much increase in U.S. manufacturing jobs, which probably means that we'll still over the long term see a decline in trend in manufacturing jobs in this area," Crone added.
According to Crone's study, more than one third of the manufacturing jobs have disappeared from the three states in the third district since 1960.
Also, Crone said that by 1992, the total number of manufacturing establishments in the region had fallen by less than 10 percent from 1963.
"Today, the average plant is producing more with fewer workers," Crone said.

The Philadelphia Fed economist also said the third district, which has traditionally been characterized as having a strong manufacturing presence, was no longer offering the same favorable conditions for new plants to be established.

"The amount of manufacturing output ... is no longer here. If you take a place like the southwest that's been growing very rapidly in terms of population, you're just going to have more plants opening there," Crone said.

The Philadelphia Fed is headed by Edward Boehne, a member of the central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Boehne is not scheduled to vote on FOMC policy actions in 1997 given the committee's rotation rules.
